item.title: nodecode-ai/nodecode
item.description:
A living agent organism in Lisp.

https://nodecode.ai

A living agent.
It becomes yours and evolves over time.

Website  ·  Docs  ·  Cells  ·  Research  ·  Discord

Cyber v1: code 2XCYBER doubles your next top-up, up to $50, until 13 Nov.
Top up  ·  Announcement


you can't read PDFs. teach yourself. It defines read-pdf, keeps it, and reads the invoice. The shell and every evaluation are real; the model's replies are scripted so the take repeats.

Nodecode is an agent that rewrites itself. It runs as one process in SBCL, a Common Lisp system, and shells attach to it. The model has one tool: it evaluates Lisp in the running program and keeps what it defines.

Install

Linux and macOS:

curl -fsSL https://nodecode.ai/install.sh | sh

Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://nodecode.ai/install.ps1 | iex

Then run nodecode. The first launch opens setup. If another coding agent lives on the machine (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes Agent, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Gemini CLI and 9 more), setup names it and asks before it reads anything; say Import and it brings over the agent's keys, instructions, memory, skills, MCP servers, bots and jobs, tick the agents one by one when it found several, or Skip and /import brings them over later. Then you pick a provider, a model and the reasoning effort. See Quickstart and First run.

What's different

Updates while it runs

An orchid opens new flowers while it keeps growing. An installed Nodecode updates itself the same way: most releases go live in the running program, one changed definition at a time, with no restart. Its own growth is kept as generations: nodecode generations lists them, nodecode rollback N restores one, and --pristine runs the binary alone. Updates


Everything is a cell

A cell is a folder that teaches Nodecode something new: a chat room it can live in, a provider login, a tool, a skill, a GitHub repo, an MCP server. nodecode add nc://cline installs one from the hub and turns it on in every attached shell. Or ask Nodecode to write one. Cells


Edits its own context

Like an organism, Nodecode decides what stays in its context and what goes, and nothing it lets go is lost. Old turns leave the window whole, never rewritten into a summary; (recall-entry N) reads any of them back word for word, and /evict makes room when you ask. The idea behind Context Language Models (Shao et al., 2026). Context and recall


Rewrites itself in Lisp

"Its programs are in the same format as its data." (John McCarthy, 1984). Code is data, so a program can rewrite itself while it runs. The model's one tool, eval, evaluates Lisp in the running Nodecode: what it defines runs at once and is kept, one file per definition, committed with git, loaded at every start. Missing a tool? It writes one. Eval and the layer


One organism, every client

The gateway is the local server every client attaches to: the terminal, a browser tab (nodecode web), your phone (/link), bots in Discord, Telegram and Slack, and programs (nodecode rpc). They all talk to the same running Nodecode, so a tool it writes in one is there in all of them.

On Linux and macOS the background gateway is on by default: it keeps Nodecode running with no shell open and starts it at login. nodecode gateway shows its state. On Windows, keep nodecode serve open in a terminal. See The gateway.

To put it in a chat room:

nodecode gateway setup discord    # or telegram, slack

It walks one channel from the bot's token to a connected bot. The token stays in a private file or an environment variable, never in the config, and the bot answers only the channels and people you allow.

Fewer tokens, same games won

On the same model, Nodecode won every public ARC-AGI-3 game with 54% fewer tokens than Claude Code (41% less cost) and 66% fewer tokens than the Codex CLI (24% less cost). The write-up: What ARC-AGI-3 costs, Foresight Labs FL-2026-006.

How the runs were measured

The 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, 183 levels, each scored with the official scorecard rule, all harnesses at xhigh reasoning. A token is every token put through the model: input, cache reads, cache writes and output. Cost uses each provider's official prices of 11 October 2026. Where a game was played more than once, the best run counts, for every harness alike. On Claude Opus 5.5, Nodecode and Claude Code both score 100. On GPT-6.1 Sol, both win all 25 games; the Codex CLI, playing through Prime Intellect's published game adapter, scores 99.9 to Nodecode's 99.5 because it took fewer actions. The GPT-6.1 Sol runs reached the model through a LiteLLM gateway and a third-party API relay.

Cells that ship with it

Turn one on with Space in /cells, or nodecode add nc://NAME:

Cell What it does
discord · telegram · slack Talk to Nodecode through a bot
web · link Use it in a browser tab with nodecode web; open that page from anywhere with /link
chrome Drive Chrome, with the companion extension
websearch Web search and page fetch, no key needed
mcp Tools from the MCP servers you list in the config
cron Prompts that run on a schedule
goal A session keeps taking turns until its goal's check passes
team · board Several sessions work one task in a shared folder; sessions on a board read each other's posts
prs Pull requests ranked and reviewed minutes after each push
experience Learns from each turn: reflections and recaps
context The always-visible context-editing skill
cyber-security The latest breaches and the fix for each, re-scanned every 6 hours; checks your server and website and walks you through patching
guard Refuses risky shell commands before they run
qa Anonymous usage counts, one page a week, sent only if you say so

More, from Nodecode and the community, are at nodecode.ai/cells. To write your own, ask Nodecode, or read the Cell API and docs/CELLS.md.

More

What does it cost?

Nodecode is free, under the MIT license. It runs on your own provider key and the provider bills you; /usage reports the spend.

Which models?

Any provider that speaks one of four wire dialects: openai-completions, openai-responses, anthropic or google. /models connects a provider from the models.dev catalog, saves its key in ~/.nodecode/auth.json and picks its model; a local server works through base_url. Its Backup tab lists the models a failing turn moves on to. See Models and providers.

Do I need to know Lisp?

No. You ask in plain words, the model writes the Lisp, and your project can be in any language. The forms it runs show on screen, and they are short.

Is it safe to run?

Nodecode ships no sandbox. eval runs Lisp and shell commands with everything your user account can do. The guard cell refuses listed risky commands, but it is not a security boundary. A cell is code with full access to your files and keys, and a message in a chat room runs with the same authority, so allowlists decide who may send one. Run it in a container or a VM before you leave it working alone. See Safety and trust.

Where does my data live?

In ~/.nodecode/: the config, your keys, every session, the cells and what the agent kept. What a turn sends goes to the provider you chose. Besides that, Nodecode checks the release feed for updates (update.mode: auto, ask or off) and reads the models.dev catalog. The qa cell sends anonymous counts only if you set it to weekly. See Files.

Which platforms?
  • Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.34 or newer: Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, RHEL 9+, Fedora 35+, Arch.
  • macOS 15+ on Apple Silicon, with Homebrew openssl@3 and zstd.
  • Windows x86_64, with Git for Windows. No background gateway: run nodecode serve instead.

No builds yet for arm64 Linux or Intel Macs. See Current support.

Update and uninstall

An installed build updates itself by default; nodecode update moves to the latest release now, and nodecode --version names the build you run. To uninstall on Linux or macOS, run nodecode gateway off, then delete ~/.local/share/nodecode/ and ~/.local/bin/nodecode. On Windows, delete %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\nodecode\ and its user PATH entry. Delete ~/.nodecode/ only to remove your sessions, keys and definitions too. See Updates.

Build from source

You need SBCL, Quicklisp, git, python3 and just.

git clone https://github.com/nodecode-ai/nodecode && cd nodecode
just test        # run the core suite
just release     # pull the shipped cells, dump ./nodecode
./nodecode

just check runs lint, the line-count ceiling, build and test. A source build doesn't update itself: pull and run just release again. To work on Nodecode itself, start with docs/README.md.

Where do I get help?

Run /doctor: it lists what is missing and prints a fix for each problem. To ask a person, join the Nodecode Discord or write to hi@nodecode.ai. See Troubleshooting.


MIT; see LICENSE. NOTICE carries the attribution for cl-tuition, which the terminal core builds on. The emblems are drawn in cells from other people's footage: the nautilus from video S2 of Barord et al., PLOS ONE 9(6): e100799, 2014, under CC BY 4.0, and John McCarthy from The Computer Chronicles, 1984, © Stewart Cheifet Productions. Every source is listed on nodecode.ai/credits.

item.title: open-goal/jak-project
item.description:
Reviving the language that brought us the Jak & Daxter Series

https://opengoal.dev

Please read first

Important

Our repositories on GitHub are for development of the project and tracking active issues. Most of the information you will find here pertains to setting up the project for development purposes and is not relevant to the end-user.

For a setup guide on how to install and play the game there is the following video that you can check out: https://youtu.be/K84UUMnkJc4

For questions or additional information pertaining to the project, we have a Discord for discussion here: https://discord.gg/VZbXMHXzWv

Additionally, you can find further documentation and answers to frequently asked questions on the project's main website: https://opengoal.dev

Warning

Do not use this decompilation project without the use of your own legally purchased copy of the game. OpenGOAL does not include any assets from the original games, so you must provide your own legitimately obtained PS2 copy of the game. OpenGOAL supports every retail PAL, NTSC, and NTSC-J build, including Greatest Hits copies. Please note that does NOT include any of the later releases (PS3/PS4/PS5).

  • Project Description
    • Current Status
    • Methodology
  • Setting up a Development Environment
    • OS Setup
    • Editor Setup
    • Building and Running the Game
      • Extract Assets
      • Build the Game (Running the Compiler)
      • Run the Game
        • Connecting the REPL to the Game
        • Running the Game Without Auto-Booting
  • Technical Project Overview

Project Description

The project's goal is to port the original trilogy (Jak 1 -> Jak 3) to PC. Over 98% of the games were written in GOAL, a custom LISP language developed by Naughty Dog. Our strategy is:

  • decompile the original game code into human-readable GOAL code
  • develop our own compiler for GOAL and recompile the game code for x86-64
  • create a tool to extract game assets into formats that can be easily viewed or modified
  • create tools to repack game assets into a format that our port uses.

Our objectives are:

  • make the port a "native application" on x86-64, with high performance. It shouldn't be emulated, interpreted, or transpiled.
  • Our GOAL compiler's performance should be around the same as unoptimized C.
  • try to match things from the original game and development as possible. For example, the original GOAL compiler supported live modification of code while the game is running, so we do the same, even though it's not required for just porting the game.
  • support modifications. It should be possible to make edits to the code without everything else breaking.

At the moment we support x86_64 on Windows, Linux and macOS (via Rosetta translation). There are no plans to ever make a mobile release.

Current Status

  • Jak 1 has been considered in a polished, complete state for years at this point.
  • Jak 2 is considered in beta due to a few issues we are aware of that need fixing, however to the casual user, the game is essentially complete.
  • Jak 3 has a good amount of work left to do.

YouTube playlist showcasing some of the early progress for Jak 1: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLWx9T30aAT50cLnCTY1SAbt2TtWQzKfXX

Methodology

To assist with decompiling, we've built a decompiler that can process GOAL code and unpack game assets. We manually specify function types and locations where we believe the original code had type casts (or where they feel appropriate) until the decompilation succeeds, then we clean up the output of the decompiled code by adding comments and adjusting formatting, then save it in goal_src/.

Our decompiler is designed specifically for processing the output of the original GOAL compiler. As a result, when given correct casts, it often produces code that can be directly fed into a compiler and works perfectly. This is continually tested as part of our unit tests.

Setting up a Development Environment

The remainder of this README is aimed at people interested in building the project from source, typically with the intention of contributing as a developer.

If this does not sound like you and you just want to play the game, refer to the above section Quick Start

OS Setup

  • Windows
  • Linux
  • MacOS
  • Docker

Editor Setup

You can of course use whatever editor you want, but here is some documentation that should help you get started on some of the editor's we have used and have written about:

  • Visual Studio (Windows)
  • Visual Studio Code
  • Zed

Building and Running the Game

Getting a running game involves 4 main steps:

  1. Build C++ tools (follow Getting Started steps above for your platform)
  2. Extract assets from the game
  3. Build the game
  4. Run the game

Extract Assets

First, we have to setup our environment so we know which game and version we are operating with. For the black label version of Jak 1 we would run the following:

task set-game-jak1
task set-decomp-ntscv1 # or for example for PAL, `task set-decomp-pal`

Run task --list to see the other available options

Next, ensure you extract your ISO file contents into the relevant iso_data/<game-name> folder. In the case of Jak 1 this is iso_data/jak1.

Once this is done, open a terminal in the jak-project folder and run the following:

task extract

Build the Game (Running the Compiler)

The next step is to build the game itself. To do so, in the same terminal run the following:

task repl

You will be greeted with a prompt like so:

 _____             _____ _____ _____ __
|     |___ ___ ___|   __|     |  _  |  |
|  |  | . | -_|   |  |  |  |  |     |  |__
|_____|  _|___|_|_|_____|_____|__|__|_____|
      |_|
Welcome to OpenGOAL 0.8!
Run (repl-help) for help with common commands and REPL usage.
Run (lt) to connect to the local target.

g >

Run the following to build the game:

g > (mi)

IMPORTANT NOTE! If you're not using the non-default version of the game, you may hit issues trying to run (mi) in this step. An example error might include something like:

Input file iso_data/jak1/MUS/TWEAKVAL.MUS does not exist.

This is because the decompiler inputs/outputs using the gameName JSON field in the decompiler config. For example if you are using Jak 1 PAL, it will assume iso_data/jak1_pal and decompiler_out/jak1_pal. Therefore, you can inform the REPL/compiler of this via the gameVersionFolder config field described here

Run the Game

Finally the game can be launched. Open a second terminal from the jak-project directory and run the following:

task boot-game

The game should boot automatically if everything was done correctly.

Connecting the REPL to the Game

Connecting the REPL to the game allows you to inspect and modify code or data while the game is running.

To do so, in the REPL after a successful (mi), run the following:

g > (lt)

If successful, your prompt should change to:

gc>

For example, running the following will print out some basic information about Jak:

gc> *target*
Running the Game Without Auto-Booting

You can also start up the game without booting. To do so run the following in one terminal

task run-game

And then in your REPL run the following (after a successful (mi)):

g > (lt)
[Listener] Socket connected established! (took 0 tries). Waiting for version...
Got version 0.8 OK!
[Debugger] Context: valid = true, s7 = 0x147d24, base = 0x2123000000, tid = 2438049

gc> (lg)
10836466        #xa559f2              0.0000        ("game" "kernel")

gc> (test-play)
(play :use-vis #t :init-game #f) has been called!
0        #x0              0.0000        0

gc>

Technical Project Overview

Some more detail about the various components of the project can be found here
